candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest predicts MALWARE with probability 1.0000, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking, but the SHAP values are small and evenly spread (+0.0068 to +0.0150). No single feature dominates. The n-grams are almost all generic stack and calling-convention patterns: SUB PUSH (+0.014968), ADD PUSH (+0.011611), LEA PUSH (+0.011485), MOV PUSH (+0.011256, frequency 0.058592), CALL PUSH (+0.011132), PUSH CALL (+0.008740), POP SUB, POP CALL, POP PUSH, POP XOR, POP TEST, POP LEA, ADD POP, MOV LEAVE and CALL RET. These look like ordinary function prologues, epilogues and argument-passing sequences, which appear in nearly any compiled x86 binary. They suggest a call-heavy, stack-based (cdecl-style) code layout, but they are not specific to mining. The only features with a plausible link to numeric workloads are MOV FLD (+0.008216, x87 floating-point loads), DIV MUL (+0.007725) and CDQ MOV (+0.013155, sign-extension before division). All three are very rare (frequencies 0.000016 to 0.000848), so they do not show the dense bitwise or arithmetic loops expected of hashing code. The evidence also lists no functions or locations where the n-grams occur, and it contains no crypto-specific mnemonic sequences such as rotate/shift/XOR chains. The model's output is therefore consistent with cryptojacking, but the listed evidence cannot confirm it independently. This is more than benign, since every contribution is positive and the model is certain, but it falls short of high confidence.
